```{python}
#| include: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from statsforecast import StatsForecast
from statsforecast.models import (MSTL, HistoricAverage, Naive,
                                  RandomWalkWithDrift, SeasonalNaive)
from statsforecast.utils import ConformalIntervals
from statsmodels.stats.diagnostic import acorr_ljungbox
from utilsforecast.losses import mase

from coursekit import datasets as D
from coursekit import plotting as P

P.use_course_style()

spine = D.spine()
H = 24
train, test = D.train_test(spine, h=H)

sf = StatsForecast(
    models=[HistoricAverage(), Naive(), SeasonalNaive(season_length=12),
            RandomWalkWithDrift()],
    freq=D.FREQ, n_jobs=1,
)
fc = sf.forecast(df=train, h=H, level=[80, 95], fitted=True)
fv = sf.forecast_fitted_values()

MODELS = ["HistoricAverage", "Naive", "SeasonalNaive", "RWD"]
LABELS = {"HistoricAverage": "Mean", "Naive": "Naive",
          "SeasonalNaive": "Seasonal naive", "RWD": "Drift"}

# --- Ch 5.7: the decomposition route, as a fifth model -------------------
from statsforecast.models import mstl, _predict_mstl_seas

sf_stl = StatsForecast(
    models=[MSTL(season_length=12, trend_forecaster=RandomWalkWithDrift())],
    freq=D.FREQ, n_jobs=1,
)
fc_stl = sf_stl.forecast(df=train, h=H, level=[80, 95])

_scored = (test.merge(fc[["unique_id", "ds", "SeasonalNaive"]], on=["unique_id", "ds"])
               .merge(fc_stl[["unique_id", "ds", "MSTL"]], on=["unique_id", "ds"]))
STL_MASE, SN_MASE = (
    float(mase(_scored, models=[m], seasonality=12, train_df=train)[m].iloc[0])
    for m in ("MSTL", "SeasonalNaive")
)

# Decomposition breakdown for visual intuition
mstl_res = mstl(train["y"].values, period=12)
dcmp_sa = mstl_res["trend"].values + mstl_res["remainder"].values
dcmp_seas = mstl_res["seasonal"].values
pred_seas = _predict_mstl_seas(mstl_res, h=H, season_length=12)
slope_sa = (dcmp_sa[-1] - dcmp_sa[0]) / (len(dcmp_sa) - 1)
pred_drift_sa = dcmp_sa[-1] + slope_sa * np.arange(1, H + 1)

# --- the three ways to draw the same interval, on one holdout -------------
resid_sn = (fv["y"] - fv["SeasonalNaive"]).dropna()

boot_paths = P.bootstrap_paths(train["y"], resid_sn, h=H, season_length=12,
                               n_paths=5000, seed=7)
boot_fan = P.paths_to_fan(fc["ds"], boot_paths, levels=(80, 95))

sf_conf = StatsForecast(
    models=[SeasonalNaive(season_length=12,
                          prediction_intervals=ConformalIntervals(n_windows=8, h=H))],
    freq=D.FREQ, n_jobs=1,
)
fc_conf = sf_conf.forecast(df=train, h=H, level=[80, 95])


def coverage_80(lo, hi, y=test["y"].to_numpy()):
    return float(((y >= np.asarray(lo)) & (y <= np.asarray(hi))).mean())


# --- and over 8 rolling origins, where a coverage rate can actually be measured
def _cv_coverage_80(model):
    cv = StatsForecast(models=[model], freq=D.FREQ, n_jobs=1).cross_validation(
        df=spine, h=12, step_size=12, n_windows=8, level=[80])
    lo, hi = cv["SeasonalNaive-lo-80"], cv["SeasonalNaive-hi-80"]
    return float(((cv["y"] >= lo) & (cv["y"] <= hi)).mean())


def _cv_coverage_80_bootstrap(pool=None):
    """pool=N restricts the draw pool to the last N residuals (the i.i.d. knob)."""
    sf_sn = StatsForecast(models=[SeasonalNaive(season_length=12)],
                          freq=D.FREQ, n_jobs=1)
    inside = []
    for w in range(8):
        end = len(spine) - (8 - w) * 12
        tr, te = spine.iloc[:end], spine.iloc[end:end + 12]
        sf_sn.forecast(df=tr, h=12, fitted=True)
        fvw = sf_sn.forecast_fitted_values()
        paths = P.bootstrap_paths(tr["y"], fvw["y"] - fvw["SeasonalNaive"], h=12,
                                  season_length=12, n_paths=5000, seed=7,
                                  resid_tail=pool)
        f = P.paths_to_fan(te["ds"], paths, levels=(80,))
        y = te["y"].to_numpy()
        inside.append((y >= f["lo-80"].to_numpy()) & (y <= f["hi-80"].to_numpy()))
    return float(np.concatenate(inside).mean())


CV_COV = {
    "Gaussian": _cv_coverage_80(SeasonalNaive(season_length=12)),
    "bootstrap": _cv_coverage_80_bootstrap(),   # full pool; see POOL_COV below
    "conformal": _cv_coverage_80(SeasonalNaive(
        season_length=12,
        prediction_intervals=ConformalIntervals(n_windows=8, h=12))),
}


def as_fan(model, frame=fc):
    return frame.rename(columns={
        model: "mean",
        f"{model}-lo-80": "lo-80", f"{model}-hi-80": "hi-80",
        f"{model}-lo-95": "lo-95", f"{model}-hi-95": "hi-95",
    })


# --- every number the prose quotes, computed, so none of it can go stale ---
from scipy.stats import kurtosis as _kurtosis

R_MEAN = float(resid_sn.mean())
R_SD_EARLY = float(resid_sn.iloc[:120].std())
R_SD_LATE = float(resid_sn.iloc[-120:].std())
GROWTH = R_MEAN / float(train["y"].mean())   # a year of growth, as a share of level

q_mean = f"{R_MEAN:+.1f}"
q_pos = f"{(resid_sn > 0).mean():.0%}"
q_n = f"{len(resid_sn)}"
q_sd1 = f"{R_SD_EARLY:.1f}"
q_sd2 = f"{R_SD_LATE:.1f}"
q_sdx = f"{R_SD_LATE / R_SD_EARLY:.0f}x"
q_kurt = f"{float(_kurtosis(resid_sn, fisher=True)):.1f}"
q_r1 = f"{float(P.acf_values(resid_sn, nlags=1)[0][0]):.2f}"
q_grow = f"{GROWTH:.0%}"

_e_lo, _e_hi = np.quantile(resid_sn, [0.1, 0.9])          # the errors' own middle 80%
_n_half = 1.2816 * float(resid_sn.std())                  # what a normal of that SD claims
q_e80, q_n80 = f"{_e_hi - _e_lo:.0f}", f"{2 * _n_half:.0f}"


def _mean_width(fan, level):
    return float(np.mean(fan[f"hi-{level}"].to_numpy() - fan[f"lo-{level}"].to_numpy()))


_gauss_fan = as_fan("SeasonalNaive")
q_wg80, q_wb80 = (f"{_mean_width(f, 80):.1f}" for f in (_gauss_fan, boot_fan))
q_wg95, q_wb95 = (f"{_mean_width(f, 95):.1f}" for f in (_gauss_fan, boot_fan))
q_narrow = f"{1 - _mean_width(boot_fan, 80) / _mean_width(_gauss_fan, 80):.0%}"

# conformal sizing, read off the ConformalIntervals(n_windows=8, h=24) above
CONF_WINDOWS = 8
q_minobs = f"{CONF_WINDOWS * H + 1}"
q_scores = f"{2 * CONF_WINDOWS}"

# the i.i.d. knob, for the note under the coverage slide
POOL_COV = {None: CV_COV["bootstrap"],
            120: _cv_coverage_80_bootstrap(pool=120),
            60: _cv_coverage_80_bootstrap(pool=60)}
q_pool_all, q_pool120, q_pool60 = (f"{POOL_COV[n]:.0%}" for n in (None, 120, 60))
```

## The Day 2 plan

Day 1 found the spine's signal is seasonality. Day 2 builds the floor a model must beat, and the way to prove a forecast is real.

::: {.incremental}
- **Four baseline models**, plus the decomposition route: the floor to beat
- **Residual diagnostics**: has the model taken all the signal?
- **Prediction intervals**: the Gaussian formula, and why it fails here
- **Two repairs**: resample the errors, then stop assuming a distribution
:::

A point forecast without an interval is an incomplete guess.

# A. The benchmark floor {.sdaia-dark background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #1C355E, #00C9A7)"}

Ch 5.1–5.2 · Simple, strong baselines

## Four benchmarks set the floor a model must clear {.smaller}

Throughout: $T$ is the last observed time, the **forecast origin**; $h$ is how many
steps ahead; $m$ is the **seasonal period**, 12 for monthly data.

::: {.incremental}
- **Mean**: $\hat{y}_{T+h} = \bar{y}$, the average of all $T$ observations
- **Naive**: $\hat{y}_{T+h} = y_T$, the last observed value
- **Seasonal naive**: $\hat{y}_{T+h} = y_{T+h-m(k+1)}$, the same month a whole
  number of years back, where $k = \lfloor (h-1)/m \rfloor$ counts the complete
  years the horizon crosses
- **Drift**: $\hat{y}_{T+h} = y_T + \dfrac{h}{T-1}(y_T - y_1)$, the line drawn
  through the first and the last observation, extended
:::

. . .

::: {.cardbox .teal}
Always fit these 4 first. On many series, **seasonal naive is tough to beat**.
:::

::: {.notes}
Do not let these sound like toys. On a seasonal series a seasonal naive is a
genuinely hard opponent, and by the end of today they will have watched it beat
a decomposition model over eight folds.

Worth saying which is which in plain language: the mean forgets time entirely,
the naive remembers only yesterday, the seasonal naive remembers this month last
year, and the drift draws a straight line through the first and last points. Ask
the room which one they expect to win here before you show them.

Two bits of the algebra pay off later, so read them out rather than skipping.
The drift denominator is T-1 because T observations have T-1 gaps between them,
which is why its interval width carries a T-1 as well. And k is 0 whenever the
horizon stays inside one year, so for h up to 12 the seasonal naive is just
"last year's same month"; k only starts counting at h = 13, and that is exactly
where its prediction interval takes its first step up. Segment C uses the same
k for the same reason.
:::

```python
# Dataset: Victorian retail takeaway turnover (train, test = D.train_test(spine, h=24))
sf = StatsForecast(freq=D.FREQ, n_jobs=1, models=[
    HistoricAverage(), Naive(), SeasonalNaive(season_length=12),
    RandomWalkWithDrift(),
])
fc = sf.forecast(df=train, h=H, level=[80, 95])

P.forecast_overlay(train, fc, MODELS, labels=LABELS, actual=test, history_tail=72)
```

:::

::: {.notes}
Point at the flat pink line first. That is the mean model, and on a series that
has grown sixfold it is visibly hopeless - which is the point of showing it. The
green naive line is flat too, but at the right level.

The orange seasonal naive is the only one with the shape of the data in it. Let
the room see that before any number is quoted.
:::

## A benchmark is what turns a score into evidence

::: {.incremental}
- **Objective evidence**: proves the complex model adds value
- **Sanity check**: catches complex ML models losing to naive rules
- **Scale baseline**: provides a standard denominator for errors (MASE)
- **Fast**: takes just a few lines of code
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-tip}
## The question to ask in every review
*"What is the simple baseline, and by how much did we beat it?"*
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the slide to slow down on if the room is senior. The question in the
callout is the one to take back to work: it costs nothing to ask, and it is the
single most effective check on a forecasting claim.

The MASE point is worth a sentence now because the metric is defined properly in
lecture 2: the benchmark is not only a rival, it is also the denominator that
makes errors comparable across series. Two slides on, a chart legend quotes MASE
numbers, and the line under it gives the room just enough to read them.
:::

## Decomposition is also a forecasting method

Ch 5.7 · You already built every step on Day 1

::: {.flowrow}
[[Series]{.flowtitle}[$y_t$]{.flownote}]{.flownode .navy}
[[STL]{.flowtitle}[splits off the season]{.flownote}]{.flownode .teal}
[[Forecast]{.flowtitle}[drift · seasonal naive]{.flownote}]{.flownode .coral}
[[Recombine]{.flowtitle}[one forecast]{.flownote}]{.flownode .purple}
:::

. . .

$$\hat{y}_{T+h} = \hat{A}_{T+h} + \hat{S}_{T+h}$$

::: {.cardbox .teal}
`MSTL(season_length=12, trend_forecaster=RandomWalkWithDrift())` runs this entire pipeline in one call.
:::

::: {.notes}
Ch 5.7. Every step is something they built yesterday: STL, the seasonally adjusted series A_t (trend + remainder), and the seasonal component S_t.
The two pieces are forecast separately (drift on A_t, seasonal naive on S_t) and added back.

The course pins trend_forecaster to drift on purpose: the default is AutoETS (Day 3), and we do not want a Day 3 model quietly winning a Day 2 comparison.

The plus sign assumes additive seasonality (swings stay constant in size). Multiplicative (swings grow with level) is handled by logging first.
:::

## How drift and seasonal naive combine inside STL

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot
```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
P.decomposition_forecast_plot(
    train, dcmp_sa, dcmp_seas, pred_drift_sa, pred_seas, fc_stl,
    actual=test, history_tail=48, figsize=(10, 4.4),
    title="Decomposition forecast: drift on deseasonalised + seasonal naive on season")
plt.show()
```

### Code
```python
# 1. Decompose into Seasonally Adjusted (A_t) and Seasonal (S_t)
# 2. Forecast A_t with Drift:             y-hat_{T+h} = A_T + h * drift_slope
# 3. Forecast S_t with Seasonal Naive:    y-hat_{T+h} = S_{T+h-m}
# 4. Recombine:                           y-hat_{T+h} = A-hat_{T+h} + S-hat_{T+h}

sf_stl = StatsForecast(
    models=[MSTL(season_length=12, trend_forecaster=RandomWalkWithDrift())],
    freq=D.FREQ, n_jobs=1,
)
fc_stl = sf_stl.forecast(df=train, h=24)
```

:::

::: {.notes}
Walk the three panels from top to bottom:
1. Top panel: Seasonally adjusted series A_t. Drift extends it with a growth line.
2. Middle panel: Seasonal component S_t. Seasonal naive repeats last year's shape.
3. Bottom panel: Summing both yields the recombined MSTL forecast (sky blue).
:::

## The decomposition route clears the floor

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot
```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
both = fc[["ds", "SeasonalNaive"]].merge(fc_stl[["ds", "MSTL"]], on="ds")
P.forecast_overlay(
    train, both, ["SeasonalNaive", "MSTL"],
    labels={"SeasonalNaive": f"Seasonal naive  (MASE {SN_MASE:.2f})",
            "MSTL": f"STL + drift  (MASE {STL_MASE:.2f})"},
    actual=test, history_tail=48, ncols=2, figsize=(10, 3.2),
    title="Spine: the floor, and the decomposition route")
plt.show()
```

### Code
```python
# Dataset: Victorian retail takeaway turnover (train, test = D.train_test(spine, h=24))
sf_stl = StatsForecast(
    models=[MSTL(season_length=12, trend_forecaster=RandomWalkWithDrift())],
    freq=D.FREQ, n_jobs=1,
)
fc_stl = sf_stl.forecast(df=train, h=H, level=[80, 95])

both = fc[["ds", "SeasonalNaive"]].merge(fc_stl[["ds", "MSTL"]], on="ds")
P.forecast_overlay(train, both, ["SeasonalNaive", "MSTL"], actual=test)
```

:::

::: {.cardbox .coral}
The seasonal naive repeats last year's **level**; STL lets drift carry the growth.
*MASE is defined in lecture 2: the error relative to a seasonal naive in-sample,
so 1.00 is the floor and lower is better.*
:::

::: {.notes}
Do not let this land as "STL wins". It wins on THIS window. Lecture 2 scores it
over eight rolling origins and the ordering flips. Flag that now, so the
reversal reads as the lesson rather than as a contradiction.
:::

# B. Residuals {.sdaia-dark background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #1C355E, #FF7A5C)"}

Ch 5.3–5.4 · Has the model finished?

## Residuals flatter, forecast errors do not

**Residual** ($e_t$): one-step error on **training** data
$$e_t = y_t - \hat{y}_{t|t-1}$$

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.cardbox}
[Residuals ($e_t$)]{.card-title}

- In-sample training errors

- **Flattering** to the model
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.cardbox .teal}
[Forecast Errors ($e_{T+h}$)]{.card-title}

- Out-of-sample holdout errors

- **Honest** evidence
:::
:::
::::

. . .

::: {.cardbox .navy}
Seasonal naive: $e_t = y_t - y_{t-12}$ (the raw year-on-year change).
:::

::: {.notes}
The holdout has not happened yet. The only evidence a model has already given you is what it got wrong on the training data.

Read yhat_{t|t-1} as "the forecast of y_t from data up to t-1" (the bar means given).

Residuals flatter, forecast errors do not. Everything in segment B is residuals. Everything in lecture 2 is forecast errors.

For a seasonal naive, the residual is simple subtraction: this March minus last March. Every number in the rest of the segment is a fact about that subtraction.
:::

## Start by looking at what the winner left behind

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot
```{python}
#| fig-width: 9.5
resid = fv["y"] - fv["SeasonalNaive"]

P.residual_time_plot(resid, ds=fv["ds"], show_mean=True, era_months=120,
                     era_labels=("first 10 years", "last 10 years"),
                     figsize=(9.5, 3.2), ylabel="residual ($M)",
                     title=f"Seasonal naive: {len(resid_sn)} one-step residuals")
plt.show()
```

### Code
```python
# fv = the training rows with fitted values attached (sf.forecast(..., fitted=True))
resid = fv["y"] - fv["SeasonalNaive"]

P.residual_time_plot(resid, ds=fv["ds"], show_mean=True, era_months=120,
                     era_labels=("first 10 years", "last 10 years"),
                     figsize=(9.5, 3.2), ylabel="residual ($M)",
                     title="Seasonal naive: 405 one-step residuals")
```

:::

::: {.incremental}
- It sits **above** zero: `{python} q_pos` of them are positive, mean `{python} q_mean`
- It **fans out**: the typical miss grew from `{python} q_sd1` to `{python} q_sd2`, `{python} q_sdx` as wide
:::

::: {.notes}
Put the figure up and say nothing for a moment. Ask the room what is wrong with
it before you reveal either bullet. Both faults are visible without a single
statistic, which is the whole reason this panel gets a slide to itself.

The first answer you will get is that it is mostly above the zero line. Good:
that is bias, and the dashed line is the mean. The second, which usually needs a
prompt, is that the left third of the picture is thin and the right third is
tall. That is the variance changing, and the two shaded stretches are the same
observation written as a number.

Say what those two SDs are, because "SD" on its own is a statistic and this is
a quantity: the shaded spans are the first ten years of residuals and the last
ten, and each SD is how far a typical month missed by inside its own span, in
the millions of dollars the y axis is drawn in. Early on the model was usually
out by about 8;
by the 2010s, by about 26. The series it is forecasting grew over the same
period, which is why the errors grew with it - the misses did not get worse
in relative terms, they got bigger in absolute ones.

Do not name the four properties yet. Two of them just walked out of the picture;
the naming slide comes after the room has seen why they exist.
:::

## The bias is the trend, arriving as an error

$e_t = y_t - y_{t-12}$, so the **mean residual is the average year-on-year gain**:

::: {.incremental}
- The spine gains about `{python} q_grow` of its average level each year, and
  `{python} q_mean` is that gain arriving one month at a time
- A seasonal naive repeats last year. It has **no term for growth**, so it hands
  the growth back as error
- This is not a bad fit. It is structure the model never had
:::

. . .

::: {.cardbox .navy}
Which is exactly why the STL + drift route beat it in segment A: **drift is the
missing term.**
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the slide that turns a diagnostic number into a diagnosis. Students can
read "+7.9" off any residual summary; what they cannot usually do is say where
it came from. Here they can, because the residual is a subtraction they
understand.

Work the arithmetic out loud. Turnover grows about 5% a year on a series
averaging 160, so a typical year adds roughly 8. The seasonal naive predicts
this March from last March, so it is short by one year of growth every single
month, and the average of those shortfalls is the mean residual. The two numbers
are the same fact.

Then land the card. Segment A showed the STL route winning the window and did
not say why. This is why. That connection is worth pausing on: the residual
check did not merely flag a problem, it named the fix, and the fix was already
on the leaderboard.

If someone asks why we do not just subtract 7.9 from every forecast: you can,
and that is a bias correction. It fixes the average and leaves the growth
unmodelled, so it is wrong again next year at a different size. Better to give
the model a trend.
:::

## The residual ACF says what is left, and what is gone

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot
```{python}
#| fig-width: 9
P.acf_plot(resid.dropna(), nlags=24, highlight_every=12, ylim=(-0.25, 1.0),
           figsize=(9, 2.8),
           title="Seasonal naive residuals, 24 lags (annual lags in orange)")
plt.show()
```

### Code
```python
# Day 1's five ACF shapes, applied to residuals instead of to a series.
P.acf_plot(resid.dropna(), nlags=24, highlight_every=12, ylim=(-0.25, 1.0),
           figsize=(9, 3.2),
           title="Seasonal naive residuals, 24 lags (annual lags in orange)")
```

:::

::: {.incremental}
- Lags 1–10 decay smoothly from `{python} q_r1`. Day 1 named that shape: **trend**
- Lags 12 and 24 (orange) fall **inside** the bounds: the season is gone
- Same fault, second instrument: the `{python} q_mean` and this decay are one missing trend
:::

::: {.notes}
Send them back to Day 1's table of five shapes before you interpret anything.
That table was built to read a series; it reads residuals with no change at all,
because residuals are just another series. Ask what shape is on the screen and
wait for someone to say slow decay.

Then make both halves of the reading count, because the orange lags are the good
news and students skate past them. Nothing at 12 or 24 means the seasonal naive
did the job it was named for: it took the season out completely. What it left is
the part it was never built to take, and that part has the trend signature.

So the two slides agree. The mean residual said the model is short by a year of
growth; the ACF says consecutive errors are short by nearly the same amount,
which is what a slowly moving level looks like. One fault, two instruments.

If asked why r_1 is so close to 1 rather than small: neighbouring months share
almost all of their shortfall, because the level moves slowly. It decays to
nothing by lag 11 because eleven months is long enough for the level to have
moved on.
:::

## Ljung-Box tests all the lags at once

Joint hypothesis test on $\ell$ residual autocorrelations:

$$Q = T(T+2)\sum_{k=1}^{\ell}\frac{r_k^2}{T-k}
\qquad Q \sim \chi^2_{\ell-K} \;\text{ under } H_0$$

::: {.incremental}
- $p < 0.05$: Autocorrelation is real $\rightarrow$ **model is not finished**
- $p \ge 0.05$: Residuals are indistinguishable from white noise
:::

```{python}
#| echo: true
r = resid.dropna()
p = acorr_ljungbox(r, lags=[24], return_df=True)["lb_pvalue"].iloc[0]
print(f"{len(r)} residuals, lag 24:  p = {p:.1e}")
```

::: {.notes}
Motivation from Day 1: With 24 individual lag bounds at 95%, expecting 1 spike by chance is normal.
Ljung-Box pools all lags into a single test:
- H_0: all autocorrelations up to lag l are zero.
- Rule of thumb: l = 24 for seasonal monthly data (2m), K = 0 for benchmarks (no estimated params).

The headline is the exponent: p = 8.6e-241 (240 zeros). The best baseline is nowhere near finished white noise. Day 3 models exist to capture this remaining signal.
:::

## Four properties, and two different repairs {.smaller}

You just failed three of them **by looking**. Each failure sends you somewhere
different.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.cardbox .teal}
[Essential: fix the model]{.card-title}

1. **Uncorrelated**: fails, slow decay  
   a pattern in the errors is signal the model never took
2. **Zero mean**: fails, mean `{python} q_mean`  
   bias, in the same direction every month
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.cardbox}
[Useful: fix the band]{.card-title}

3. **Constant variance**: fails, spread `{python} q_sd1` then `{python} q_sd2`  
   one spread number sizes the band for every era
4. **Normal**: not yet checked  
   it sets the multiplier that widens the band
:::
:::
::::

. . .

::: {.cardbox .navy}
The left column failed and segment A already showed the repair. **The rest of
this deck repairs the right column** by changing the interval, not the series.
fpp3's other route, a log or Box-Cox transform, is Day 3's.
:::

::: {.notes}
This slide is a summary, not an introduction. Everything in the left column and
item 3 on the right was derived on the previous four slides, so read the
verdicts off rather than re-teaching them. The only new line is normality, and
it is deliberately unmarked: segment C opens with it.

Say the split as an instruction rather than as a taxonomy. A left-column failure
is a message about the model: go back and change it. A right-column failure
leaves the point forecast alone and tells you the band around it is wrong. A
model can pass the left column and fail the right.

The right column is worth saying out loud as a pair, because both feed one
formula: the band is a spread number times a multiplier. Constant variance is
what lets a single spread number stand for the whole history; normality is what
makes the multiplier the right size. Fail either and the width is wrong while
the centre is fine.

One honest caveat if someone asks: uncorrelated appears on both sides. It is
essential for the model, and it is also one of the three assumptions behind the
Gaussian interval, which segment C spells out.

Expect a stats-literate room to reach for a transform before you offer it, so
have the answer ready. Taking logs, or a Box-Cox with the spine's lambda of
about 0.07, would stop the spread growing with the level and move item 3 out of
the right column entirely. It is a real fix and it is deliberately not today's:
today is about what to do when the band is wrong, and Day 3 opens with the
transform.

Segments C, D and E are, in order, the three ways to stop relying on the right
column. Lab exercise 2.2 runs this same checklist on the drift method and asks
them to write the verdict.
:::

# C. Prediction intervals {.sdaia-dark background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #1C355E, #9B8EC0)"}

Ch 5.5 · Quantifying uncertainty

## A range is what a decision can act on

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.cardbox}
[Point forecast]{.card-title}

*"Demand will be 340 units."*

- Guaranteed to be wrong
- Hides the operational risk
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.cardbox .teal}
[Interval forecast]{.card-title}

*"Demand: [300, 380], 80% of the time."*

- Sizes the safety stock
- States the risk out loud
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Decisions like staffing buffers, warehouse capacity, and safety inventory depend directly on the interval width.
:::

## The future is a range, not a point

At forecast origin $T$ the future value is still random. Capital $Y$ marks a value
that has not been observed yet; lowercase $y$ one that has:

$$Y_{T+h}\mid \mathcal{I}_T
\qquad \mathcal{I}_T = \text{everything known at time } T$$

::: {.incremental}
- **Forecast distribution:** plausible future values, given what is known at $T$
- **Point forecast:** one centre, usually a mean or median
- **80% interval:** 10th to 90th percentile
- **95% interval:** 2.5th to 97.5th percentile
:::

. . .

::: {.cardbox .teal}
The **unknown future value**, not the prediction, is represented by a distribution.
:::

::: {.notes}
Start with what is uncertain. We produce one point forecast, but we do not
believe the future must equal that point. Before it is observed, we represent
the future as plausible outcomes conditional on what we know now.

The point forecast is one summary. An interval takes two quantiles. The rest of
the deck asks how to construct them: impose a Gaussian shape, simulate futures
from empirical errors, or calibrate a set from past forecast errors.
:::

## Gaussian intervals impose a shape

$$\hat{\sigma} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{T - K - M}\sum_{t=1}^{T} e_t^2}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\hat{y}_{T+1|T} \pm c\,\hat{\sigma}$$

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.cardbox}
[Residual Spread $\hat{\sigma}$]{.card-title}

- $K$: parameters estimated (0 for benchmarks)

- $M$: missing residuals (e.g. 12 for seasonal naive)

- Dividing by $T$ makes $\hat{\sigma}$ too small
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.cardbox .teal}
[Normal Multiplier $c$]{.card-title}

- **80% interval**: $c = 1.28$

- **95% interval**: $c = 1.96$

- Exact **only if** residuals are normal

:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
The M term is where people trip: a seasonal naive cannot produce fitted values for its first 12 months, so 12 residuals are missing (405 residuals, not 417). Undercounting missing values makes sigma-hat too small and intervals too narrow.

The multiplier c assumes standard normality. If residuals have fat tails or skew, 1.28 is the wrong multiplier.
Segment D (bootstrap) and Segment E (conformal) solve this.
:::

## How fast the range widens depends on the method

| Benchmark | $h$-step forecast standard deviation |
|---|---|
| Mean | $\hat{\sigma}_h = \hat{\sigma}\sqrt{1 + 1/T}$ |
| Naive | $\hat{\sigma}_h = \hat{\sigma}\sqrt{h}$ |
| Seasonal naive | $\hat{\sigma}_h = \hat{\sigma}\sqrt{k+1}$, &nbsp; $k = \lfloor (h-1)/m \rfloor$ |
| Drift | $\hat{\sigma}_h = \hat{\sigma}\sqrt{h\left(1 + \dfrac{h}{T-1}\right)}$ |

. . .

::: {.cardbox .teal}
**Seasonal naive width is a staircase**: flat within each year ($h \le 12$), stepping up only when crossing into another full cycle ($k+1$).
:::

::: {.notes}
All four formulas assume the residuals are uncorrelated. That assumption is
already known to be false here - segment B just rejected it at p ~ 1e-240.

Two of the four are readable straight off their point forecasts, so read them
off. The mean's 1 + 1/T is one variance for the noise plus one T-th for not
knowing the true mean. The drift's T-1 is the T-1 gaps its slope was averaged
over, the same T-1 that is in its point forecast; the more history the slope
came from, the less the extrapolation adds.
:::

## The interval is the forecast, the line is its middle

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot
```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
P.fan_chart(train, as_fan("SeasonalNaive"), levels=(80, 95), actual=test,
            history_tail=72, figsize=(10, 4.6),
            title="Seasonal naive: 80% and 95% prediction intervals")
plt.show()
```

### Code
```python
# Dataset: Victorian retail takeaway turnover (train, test = D.train_test(spine, h=24))
# as_fan() renames one model's columns to ds / mean / lo-L / hi-L.
fc = sf.forecast(df=train, h=H, level=[80, 95])

P.fan_chart(train, as_fan("SeasonalNaive"), levels=(80, 95), actual=test,
            history_tail=72)
```

:::

::: {.notes}
Make the room read the dashed actual line against the bands rather than admiring
the shading. Ask how many of the 24 points fall inside the 80% band. It looks
excellent here, and lecture 2 shows that a single 24-point window cannot measure
a coverage rate at all.

If you want one sentence for this slide: the interval is the forecast, and the
line down the middle is just its most likely value.
:::


## The Gaussian interval rests on three assumptions

::: {.incremental}
1. Residuals are **uncorrelated**: otherwise $\hat{\sigma}$ understates the spread
2. Residuals have **constant variance**: one $\hat{\sigma}$ for the whole series
3. Residuals are **normally distributed**: otherwise $c = 1.28$ is the wrong multiplier
:::

. . .

::: {.cardbox .navy}
Segment B failed the first two **by looking.** The third has never been checked.
:::

::: {.notes}
Count them off on your fingers, because the next two segments buy them back one
at a time and it helps if the room is counting with you. Two of the three were
measured in segment B - the slow decay, and the SD tripling across the eras.
The third, normality, is the one segment B left open, and the next slide closes
it. Bootstrap buys back normality. Conformal avoids specifying a distributional
shape, but replaces those assumptions with exchangeability. Distribution-free
never means assumption-free.
:::

## Normality fails too, and it makes the band too wide

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot
```{python}
#| fig-width: 9
P.residual_assumption_plot(resid_sn, ds=fv["ds"], window=36, level=80,
                           figsize=(9.5, 2.7))
plt.show()
```

### Code
```python
# Left:  a rolling 36-month SD against the single pooled sigma-hat.
# Right: the residual histogram against a normal of the SAME SD, with the
#        empirical (blue) and normal (orange) central-80% cut points drawn on.
P.residual_assumption_plot(resid_sn, ds=fv["ds"], window=36, level=80)
```

:::

::: {.incremental}
- Excess kurtosis `{python} q_kurt`: a sharp peak with fat tails, not a normal
- The errors' own middle 80% (blue) spans `{python} q_e80`; $c = 1.28$ claims `{python} q_n80`
:::

::: {.cardbox .navy}
All three assumptions fail. The next two methods each buy one of them back.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the check segment B put off, and it closes the loop on the four
properties: normality was item 4, and it was the only one left unmarked.

Read the panels as a pair. The left one is constant variance, failing in the
plainest way a picture can fail: a rolling SD that climbs while the pooled
sigma-hat sits flat through the middle of it. One number is standing in for a
spread that tripled, so it is too big for the 1980s and too small for the 2010s.

The right one is normality. Excess kurtosis is 0 for a normal; this is nearly 6,
and the histogram shows why - a peak far sharper than the curve, and tails
outside it. Then point at the two pairs of vertical lines, because that is where
the abstraction turns into money. Orange is where a normal of this SD puts the
central 80%; blue is where these errors actually put it. Blue is the narrower
pair, about a fifth narrower, which is exactly the width segment D's bootstrap
comes back with.

Blue is also off-centre, and someone will spot it. That is the +7.9 bias again:
these errors are not centred on zero, so their middle 80% is not either. A
symmetric plus-or-minus cannot represent that at all.

Worth saying that the fat tails cut the other way further out: at 95% the
errors' own span is about a tenth WIDER than the normal's. Sharp peak, fat
tails, so the 80% band shrinks and the 95% band does not. That is the punchline
of the bootstrap comparison two slides on, and saying it here makes it a
confirmation rather than a surprise.
:::

# D. Bootstrapped intervals {.sdaia-dark background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #1C355E, #00C9A7)"}

Ch 5.5 · Dropping the normality assumption

::: {.notes}
Roughly 33 minutes into the deck, with about 22 still to run before the real
break at the deck boundary. Take two minutes here and let the room stand up.
Segments D and E are the densest stretch of Day 2, and they land better on a
room that has moved.
:::

## Resample the errors you actually saw

Stop assuming a bell curve. Use the `{python} q_n` errors the model already
made: **draw one at random, add it, step forward, repeat.**

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.cardbox .teal}
[Naive: last month + an error]{.card-title}

$y_t = y_{t-1} + e_t$

$$y^*_{T+1} = y_T + e^*_{T+1}$$
$$y^*_{T+2} = y^*_{T+1} + e^*_{T+2}$$
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.cardbox}
[Seasonal naive: last year + an error]{.card-title}

$y_t = y_{t-m} + e_t$

$$y^*_{T+i} = y^*_{T+i-m} + e^*_{T+i}$$
:::
:::
::::

::: {.cardbox .navy}
$e^*$: a past residual, drawn **with replacement** · $y^*$: one path out to
$h$, which is one possible future
:::

::: {.notes}
Say the idea before the algebra. Every one of these models says the next value
is something we already know plus an error: e_t = y_t - yhat_{t|t-1} rearranges
to y_t = yhat_{t|t-1} + e_t. Segment C filled that error in from a formula, by
assuming it was normal with SD sigma-hat. We have just seen that it is not
normal. So fill it in from the 405 errors the model actually made instead:
put them in a hat, pull one out, write it down, put it back.

With replacement is the part to say out loud. There are 405 residuals and we
want 5000 futures of 24 months each, which is 120000 draws; the same past error
turns up many times, and that is fine, because we are treating those 405 as a
sample of the errors this model makes rather than as a list of what will happen.

Then read the two columns as the same recipe on two different lags. The naive
adds an error to last month, the seasonal naive to last year. Repeat 24 times
and you have one path; the next slide runs it 5000 times.

The seeding detail is the mechanism behind the fan, and it is worth the extra
sentence. The first twelve simulated months each hang off a real observed value
plus one drawn error, so they scatter by about one error's worth. Month 13 hangs
off simulated month 1, so it carries that error plus a new one, and from there
the errors accumulate. That is the fan, and it is why the band steps out at
exactly the same place the closed-form staircase does.
:::

## The assumption you just made

::: {.cardbox .teal}
[Core Assumption: Identical Distribution]{.card-title}
Residuals are assumed to come from a single fixed pool $\hat{F}$ that does not change over time (i.i.d. draws).
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.cardbox}
[What you bought]{.card-title}

- **Normality dropped**: uses true error shape
- Skew and kurtosis handled naturally
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.cardbox .navy}
[What you still owe]{.card-title}

- **Identical distribution**: fails as SD tripled
- Pooling old and new residuals hurts coverage
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
The bootstrap trades normality for identical distribution. On this series that trade fails if we pool all years because residual spread tripled.
Restricting the bootstrap to recent residuals (the i.i.d. knob) restores coverage from ~61% to ~87-91%.
:::

## 5000 possible futures

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot
```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
P.sim_paths_plot(train, fc["ds"], boot_paths, n_show=8, history_tail=60,
                 actual=test, figsize=(10, 3.4),
                 title="Eight of the 5000 simulated sample paths")
plt.show()
```

### Code
```python
# Dataset: Victorian retail takeaway turnover, seasonal naive residuals
resid_sn = (fv["y"] - fv["SeasonalNaive"]).dropna()

boot_paths = P.bootstrap_paths(train["y"], resid_sn, h=24, season_length=12,
                               n_paths=5000, seed=7)     # -> (5000, 24)
P.sim_paths_plot(train, fc["ds"], boot_paths, n_show=8, actual=test)
```

:::

::: {.cardbox .teal}
The band is not the method. The **paths** are the method; the band is a
percentile taken down each column.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the slide that fixes the most common misconception about the bootstrap.
Students see the shaded band and assume the band is the method. It is not. The
method is these paths; the band is a percentile taken down each column
afterwards.

Trace one path with your finger from the origin out to 24 months, and say: this
is one possible future, drawn by taking last year's value and adding a real
error we actually observed at some point in the past.
:::

## Dropping normality buys a fifth off the 80% band

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot
```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
P.fan_chart_panels(train, [as_fan("SeasonalNaive"), boot_fan],
                   titles=("Gaussian, plus/minus c sigma-hat",
                           "Bootstrap, 5000 paths"),
                   levels=(80, 95), actual=test, history_tail=36,
                   colors=[P.ORANGE, P.ORANGE], figsize=(10, 3.3))
plt.show()
```

### Code
```python
# boot_fan = P.paths_to_fan(fc["ds"], boot_paths, levels=(80, 95))
#   -> ds / mean / lo-80 / hi-80 / lo-95 / hi-95, from empirical percentiles
P.fan_chart(train, as_fan("SeasonalNaive"), levels=(80, 95), actual=test)
P.fan_chart(train, boot_fan, levels=(80, 95), actual=test)
```

:::

::: {.incremental}
- Mean **80%** width: `{python} q_wg80` Gaussian vs **`{python} q_wb80`** bootstrap, `{python} q_narrow` narrower
- Mean **95%** width: `{python} q_wg95` vs **`{python} q_wb95`**, the gap has closed
- Sharp peak, fat tails. That is what an excess kurtosis of `{python} q_kurt` buys you
:::

::: {.notes}
Same model, same point forecast, same data. Only the assumption changed, and the
80% band got a fifth narrower.

Notice the 95% bands barely differ. That is the shape of the residuals showing
up exactly where you would expect it: the sharp peak makes the central 80%
tighter, and the fat tails put the 95% back where the normal had it.
:::

# E. Conformal prediction {.sdaia-dark background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #1C355E, #FF7A5C)"}

Ch 5.5 · Distribution-free intervals, and the only method that
works on a model with no formula

## Name the error first: $e_{t+h|t}$

$$e_{t+h|t} = y_{t+h} - \hat{y}_{t+h|t}$$

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.cardbox}
[Indices]{.card-title}

- $t$: Forecast **origin** (when made)
- $h$: Forecast **horizon** (steps ahead)
- $t+h$: Future time being predicted
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.cardbox .teal}
[Residual vs Horizon Error]{.card-title}

- $h = 1$: Standard 1-step residual
- $h > 1$: Out-of-sample error, **collected across rolling origins**
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Notation discipline pays off here. e_{t+h|t} carries two indices for a reason:
which point is being forecast, and which origin it was forecast from. A 12-step error made in 2010 and a 12-step error made in 2016 are two members of the same calibration set.

Residuals had one index because there was only ever one origin: yesterday. For h > 1, errors must be collected, not fitted.
:::

## A worked example of $e_{t+h|t}$

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Walk-through
You hold $y_1, y_2, \dots, y_{10}$ and want a **3-step-ahead** interval.

::: {.incremental}
1. Stand at $t = 5$. Pretend $y_6 \dots y_{10}$ do not exist yet.
2. Forecast three steps out: $\hat{y}_{8|5}$.
3. Now look up what really happened: $y_8$.
4. Record $e_{{8|5}} = y_8 - \hat{{y}}_{{8|5}}$, one 3-step-ahead error.
:::

Slide the origin to $t = 6, 7, \dots$ and repeat. What you collect is the
**calibration set** for $h = 3$.

### Plot
```{python}
#| fig-width: 9
toy = pd.DataFrame({"ds": np.arange(1, 11),
                    "y": [10., 12, 11, 14, 13, 16, 15, 18, 17, 20]})
toy_err = pd.DataFrame([
    {"cutoff": t, "ds": t + 3,
     "y": toy["y"].iloc[t + 2],       # y_{t+3}
     "yhat": toy["y"].iloc[t - 1]}    # naive: y-hat_{t+3|t} = y_t
    for t in (5, 6, 7)
])
P.h_step_error_diagram(toy, toy_err, figsize=(9, 3.9), xticks=range(1, 11),
                       title="Three 3-step-ahead errors, from three origins")
plt.show()
```

:::

::: {.notes}
Walk this by hand on the numbers. Stand at t=5, the naive forecast for t=8 is
whatever y_5 was, then look up what actually happened at t=8 and subtract.
That single number is one member of the calibration set.

Slide the origin forward and you get another. Conformal prediction is nothing
more elaborate than collecting those and taking a quantile of their absolute
values.
:::

## Distribution-free is not assumption-free

::: {.cardbox .teal}
[Core Requirement: Exchangeability]{.card-title}
Calibration errors and the next test error must be **exchangeable** (order invariant).
:::

Empirical quantile of collected absolute errors:
$$\hat{y}_{T+h|T} \pm Q_{1-\alpha}\big(|e_{t+h|t}|\big)$$

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.cardbox}
[Per-Horizon Width]{.card-title}
One quantile per $h$: interval growth with horizon is **measured**, not assumed
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.cardbox .navy}
[Distribution-Free]{.card-title}
No $\hat{\sigma}$, no normal table, no parametric distribution required
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Exchangeability asks whether the calibration errors and the next error remain comparable when their order is shuffled. It permits dependence that i.i.d. forbids, but does not excuse a changing regime (e.g. non-constant variance over decades).

Because the interval is an empirical quantile of actual model errors, there is no sigma-hat to estimate and no normal table to look up.
That is why conformal intervals work on models that have no closed-form formula (ML models, neural nets, Day 3).
:::

## Where the calibration set comes from

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot
```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
cs = sf.cross_validation(df=train, h=12, step_size=12, n_windows=4)
cs12 = (cs[cs["ds"] == cs["cutoff"] + pd.DateOffset(months=12)]
        .rename(columns={"SeasonalNaive": "yhat"})[["cutoff", "ds", "y", "yhat"]])
P.h_step_error_diagram(train.tail(84), cs12, figsize=(10, 4.2),
                       title="Four origins, h = 12: the errors conformal quantifies")
plt.show()
```

### Code
```python
# Roll the origin backwards; keep the error at the horizon you care about.
cs = sf.cross_validation(df=train, h=12, step_size=12, n_windows=4)
cs12 = (cs[cs["ds"] == cs["cutoff"] + pd.DateOffset(months=12)]
        .rename(columns={"SeasonalNaive": "yhat"})[["cutoff", "ds", "y", "yhat"]])
P.h_step_error_diagram(train.tail(84), cs12)
```

:::

::: {.notes}
statsforecast does exactly this internally: n_windows rolling origins, the
absolute error at each horizon, then the empirical quantile of those.
:::

## Any model at all can be given a conformal interval {.smaller}

```python
from statsforecast.utils import ConformalIntervals

sf_conf = StatsForecast(
    models=[SeasonalNaive(
        season_length=12,
        prediction_intervals=ConformalIntervals(n_windows=8, h=24),
    )],
    freq="MS",
)
fc_conf = sf_conf.forecast(df=train, h=24, level=[80, 95])
```

::: {.incremental}
- `n_windows`: how many rolling origins make up the calibration set
- Wants `n_windows` $\times\,h + 1$ observations (`{python} q_minobs` here). Given fewer it
  **silently** fits as many windows as it can, and only errors below $2h + 1$
- It mirrors each horizon's 8 absolute errors to $\hat{y} \pm |e|$ and takes the
  quantile of those **`{python} q_scores`** values, so the band is **visibly jittery**
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the practical payoff of the whole segment and the thing a Day 3 author
will need: any model that has no closed-form interval gets one from
prediction_intervals=ConformalIntervals(...). Not every statsforecast model can
produce intervals on its own; all of them can produce conformal ones.

The jitter warning is worth making concrete. Eight rolling origins give eight
absolute errors per horizon; statsforecast reflects each one to both sides of
the point forecast and takes the quantile of the sixteen values that makes,
which is why the slide says sixteen where the room will have counted eight. The
band wobbles because sixteen numbers is a small sample, not because anything is
broken.

The sizing bullet matters more than it looks. n_windows is a request, not a
setting: statsforecast quietly takes min(n_windows, (n-1)//h) and only raises if
that falls below 2. Ask for 8 windows at h=24 on a series of 200 points and you
get 8; on 150 you silently get 6, with no warning anywhere. Anyone taking this
to Day 3 or to work should check what they actually got.
:::

## One point forecast, three different bands

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot
```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
BANDS = {
    "Gaussian": (fc["SeasonalNaive-lo-80"], fc["SeasonalNaive-hi-80"]),
    "Bootstrap": (boot_fan["lo-80"], boot_fan["hi-80"]),
    "Conformal": (fc_conf["SeasonalNaive-lo-80"], fc_conf["SeasonalNaive-hi-80"]),
}
P.interval_bounds_plot(train, fc["ds"], BANDS, actual=test, history_tail=24,
                       level=80, figsize=(10, 2.8),
                       titles=("80% bounds, same point forecast",
                               "Staircase, narrow, and jittery"))
plt.show()
```

### Code
```python
# One model, three interval methods, on the same axes.
# fc       - Gaussian, from sf.forecast(..., level=[80, 95])
# boot_fan - P.paths_to_fan(fc["ds"], boot_paths)
# fc_conf  - SeasonalNaive(prediction_intervals=ConformalIntervals(n_windows=8, h=24))
BANDS = {
    "Gaussian": (fc["SeasonalNaive-lo-80"], fc["SeasonalNaive-hi-80"]),
    "Bootstrap": (boot_fan["lo-80"], boot_fan["hi-80"]),
    "Conformal": (fc_conf["SeasonalNaive-lo-80"], fc_conf["SeasonalNaive-hi-80"]),
}
P.interval_bounds_plot(train, fc["ds"], BANDS, actual=test)
```

:::

**Coverage**: the share of the actual values that landed inside the band.

```{python}
#| echo: false
rows = []
for lab, lo, hi in [
    ("Gaussian", fc["SeasonalNaive-lo-80"], fc["SeasonalNaive-hi-80"]),
    ("Bootstrap", boot_fan["lo-80"], boot_fan["hi-80"]),
    ("Conformal", fc_conf["SeasonalNaive-lo-80"], fc_conf["SeasonalNaive-hi-80"]),
]:
    rows.append({"method": lab,
                 "mean 80% width": float(np.mean(np.asarray(hi) - np.asarray(lo))),
                 "coverage (24 pts)": coverage_80(lo, hi)})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False,
      formatters={"mean 80% width": "{:.1f}".format,
                  "coverage (24 pts)": "{:.0%}".format}))
```

::: {.notes}
One point forecast, three bands. Left panel says they are not the same object;
right panel says how they differ in shape. Gaussian is the staircase, bootstrap
is narrow, conformal is jittery.

The printed numbers are the trap, so read them out and then say plainly where
they came from: 24 points. The next slide is the arithmetic on why that cannot
separate three methods.
:::

## Every interval method spends an assumption

| Method | Assumes | Gives |
|---|---|---|
| Gaussian | uncorrelated · constant variance · **normal** | closed form |
| Bootstrap | uncorrelated · **i.i.d. from $\hat{F}$** | any error shape |
| Conformal | **exchangeable** $h$-step errors | no parametric shape |

::: {.callout-important}
Pick by which assumption you can defend, not by the widths on the last slide.
:::

::: {.notes}
The table is the takeaway. Each row is a trade, and the honest question when
choosing is not "which is most accurate" but "which of these three assumptions
am I willing to make about this series".

If the room wants a default: conformal, because it assumes least, and because it
is the one that generalises to models that have no formula. That is also why it
is the one Day 3 will lean on. But say the qualification out loud: its interval
is distribution-free, not assumption-free, and a changing error regime can
break exchangeability.
:::

## Why one test window is misleading

$$\text{SE} = \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.8 \times 0.2}{24}} \approx 8\%
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\text{95% CI on 80% coverage: } [64\%, 96\%]$$

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.cardbox .navy}
[Single Holdout ($n = 24$)]{.card-title}
Coverage measures **96%** by chance alone. You cannot validate coverage on a single slice.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.cardbox .teal}
[8-Fold CV ($n = 96$)]{.card-title}

- **Gaussian**: 77%
- **Bootstrap**: 61%
- **Conformal**: 83%

*Methods separate cleanly.*
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
A nominal 80% interval easily measures anywhere from 64% to 96% on a single 24-point holdout by chance alone (and points clump rather than being independent coin flips).

The bootstrap's 61% is the i.i.d. assumption being punished: pooling 1980s residuals (SD 8.5) with 2010s (SD 26.2) makes the draw pool too tight. Restricting the pool to recent residuals restores coverage to ~87-91%.

Over 8 rolling origins, we actually get enough points to evaluate reliability.
:::
